title: 2016 AMC 12B 22
statement: For a certain positive integer \(n\) less than \(1000,\) the decimal equivalent of \(\dfrac1n\) is \(0.\overline{abcdef},\) a repeating decimal of period \(6,\) and the decimal equivalent of \(\dfrac{1}{n+6}\) is \(0.\overline{wxyz},\) a repeating decimal of period \(4.\) In which interval does \(n\) lie?

solutions.text:
Period \(6\) requires \(10^6-1=3^3\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot37\) to be divisible by \(n.\) Period \(4\) requires \(10^4-1=3^2\cdot11\cdot101\) to be divisible by \(n+6,\) while \(10^2-1=3^2\cdot11\) is not divisible by \(n+6\) (else the period would be \(1\) or \(2\)). Hence \(n+6\) is a multiple of \(101.\) Since \(n+6\) also divides \(3^2\cdot11\cdot101\) and is less than \(1006,\) the only possibilities are \(n+6=101,303,909,\) giving \(n=95,297,903.\) Only \(297=3^3\cdot11\) divides \(10^6-1,\) so \(n=297.\)

Finally, \(10^6\equiv1\pmod{297},\) while \(10^2\not\equiv1\) and \(10^3\not\equiv1\pmod{297},\) so its period is exactly \(6.\) Also \(303\) divides \(10^4-1\) but not \(10^2-1,\) so the period of \(\frac{1}{303}\) is exactly \(4.\) Thus \(n=297\) lies in \([201,400].\)

Thus, the correct answer is B.
hints: Period \(6\) means \(10^6-1=3^3\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot37\) is divisible by \(n;\) period \(4\) means \(10^4-1=3^2\cdot11\cdot101\) is divisible by \(n+6\)
\(n+6\) must divide \(10^4-1\) but not \(10^2-1,\) forcing \(n+6=101k;\) test each \(n=101k-6\lt1000\) to see whether \(10^6-1\) is divisible by \(n\)
